content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is a rare condition that follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. It is one of the leading causes of death in infants, particularly those aged between one month and one year, in the United States. In 1830, Kopp proposed the concept of thymic asthma, suggesting that an enlarged thymus could lead to the death of a child. During the 18th century, other theories emerged, attributing sudden infant deaths to asphyxial mechanisms, suffocation, catarrh, superstitions, or even the actions of witches and gods. The term sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) was first introduced by Horgan in 1969. By 1971, SIDS was officially recognized as a valid diagnosis on death certificates. In 1979, the World Health Organization (WHO) assigned a unique code (798.0) to SIDS within the International Classification of Diseases. In 1982, Kelly and colleagues were the first to identify apneic episodes in newborn siblings of infants who had died from SIDS. In 1986, Bass and colleagues reported that accidental asphyxiation in infants could result from objects in the crib or violent shaking, which could lead to a severe condition known as shaken baby syndrome. That same year, Smialek documented cases of infant twins who died suddenly and simultaneously. In 1990, the Back to Sleep campaign was introduced, which led to a significant reduction in SIDS cases. In 1992, Filiano and Kinney identified a link between developmental hypoplasia of the arcuate nucleus and the occurrence of SIDS. In 1995, Pinholster described breathing patterns and conditions that could predispose infants to SIDS. In 2004, Mage and Donner provided detailed explanations of infant respiratory mortality in regions such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and Scandinavia.
